learn: Our solar system has one star, the Sun, and eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
The four inner planets are small and rocky. The four outer planets are giant worlds made mostly of gas and ice.
The solar system also holds dwarf planets like Pluto, moons, asteroids and comets.
check: How many planets are in our solar system?
lessons.try: Make a scale model of planet distances using a long strip of paper.

learn: Gravity is a force of attraction between all objects that have mass.
The more mass an object has, the stronger its pull. The farther apart objects are, the weaker the pull.
The Sun's gravity keeps the planets in orbit. Earth's gravity keeps the Moon in orbit.
check: Gravity gets weaker when objects are...
What keeps planets orbiting the Sun?
lessons.try: Swing a ball on a string in a circle and explain how the string acts like gravity.

learn: Space distances are huge. Scientists use the astronomical unit (AU), the average Earth-Sun distance of about 150 million km.
Neptune is about 30 AU from the Sun.
Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
check: One AU is the distance from...
Neptune is about ___ AU from the Sun.
lessons.try: Calculate how many times farther Neptune is from the Sun than Earth.

learn: For centuries many people believed Earth was the centre (geocentric model), as Ptolemy described.
Copernicus (1543) proposed the sun at the centre; Galileo's telescope found Jupiter's moons and Venus's phases as evidence.
Models change when new evidence appears.
lessons.try: Compare the two models in a T-chart with evidence.

learn: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are small, rocky and close to the sun.
Venus is the hottest because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.
Mars has the tallest volcano, Olympus Mons.
lessons.try: Make fact cards for the four inner planets.

learn: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are giant planets made mostly of gas and ice.
All four have rings and many moons.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm larger than Earth.
check: The Great Red Spot is a...
lessons.try: Compare the giant planets in a table.

learn: Pluto is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt.
The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.
Comets are icy bodies that grow tails near the sun.
check: The asteroid belt is between Mars and...
lessons.try: Map where small bodies are found.

learn: Earth has one moon; Jupiter and Saturn have dozens.
Europa may hide an ocean under its ice.
Titan has lakes of liquid methane.
lessons.try: Research one moon and present it.

learn: Every mass pulls on every other mass.
More mass means stronger pull; more distance means weaker pull.
Gravity keeps planets in orbit.
lessons.try: Model gravity with a stretched sheet and marbles.

learn: A planet moves forward (inertia) while gravity pulls it in.
The balance makes a curved orbit.
Without gravity it would fly off in a straight line.
check: Without gravity a planet would move in a...
lessons.try: Swing a ball on a string and let go.

learn: Johannes Kepler found that orbits are ellipses (stretched circles).
Planets move faster when closer to the sun.
Outer planets take longer to orbit.
check: Planets move faster when ___ the sun.
lessons.try: Draw an ellipse with two pins and string.

learn: Weight depends on a planet's gravity.
A 40 kg student weighs about 0.38 times as much on Mars.
Mass stays the same.
check: On Mars you weigh about ___ of Earth weight.
lessons.try: Calculate your weight on five worlds.

learn: 1 AU is the Earth–sun distance, about 150 million km.
Jupiter is about 5.2 AU from the sun.
AU makes big numbers easier.
lessons.try: Build a scale model with AU on a hallway.

learn: Probes like Voyager have left the solar system.
Rovers explore Mars.
Telescopes in space see farther without air blurring.
lessons.try: Make a timeline of five space missions.

learn: Inner rocky, outer giant planets.
Gravity and inertia make orbits.
Small bodies and moons.
check: The planet closest to the sun is...
Orbits are shaped by gravity and...
lessons.try: Solar system trivia relay.

units.t: Earth, Moon and Sun: Seasons, Phases and Eclipses

learn: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees.
As Earth orbits the Sun, each hemisphere takes turns tilting toward the Sun, getting more direct light and longer days: summer.
Seasons are not caused by distance from the Sun. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January.
check: When it is summer in the north, the south has...
lessons.try: Use a lamp and a tilted ball to show summer in each hemisphere.

learn: The Moon does not make its own light; it reflects sunlight.
As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of its lit half: new, crescent, quarter, gibbous and full.
A full cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days.
check: A full cycle of phases takes about...
When we see none of the lit side, it is a...
lessons.try: Draw the Moon every night for two weeks and label each phase.

learn: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, blocking sunlight.
A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes between the Sun and Moon, casting a shadow on the Moon.
Never look directly at the Sun, even during an eclipse; use certified eclipse glasses or a pinhole viewer.
check: In a solar eclipse, what is in the middle?
In a lunar eclipse, what casts the shadow?
Safe ways to view a solar eclipse include...
lessons.try: Use a lamp, ball and marble to model both kinds of eclipse.

learn: Rotation: Earth spins in 24 hours. Revolution: orbits in about 365.25 days.
The extra quarter day gives leap years.
Rotation makes day and night.
check: Leap years fix the extra ___ day.
lessons.try: Model both motions with a lamp and globe.

learn: Earth's axis tilts 23.5°.
Direct rays heat more than slanted rays.
The hemisphere tilted towards the sun gets direct rays: summer.
check: Direct rays heat ___ than slanted rays.
Summer comes when your hemisphere tilts ___ the sun.
lessons.try: Shine a torch straight and slanted at graph paper.

learn: Summer solstice: longest day (about June 21 in the north).
Winter solstice: shortest day (about December 21).
Equinoxes: equal day and night (March and September).
check: The longest day is the ___ solstice.
Equal day and night happens at an...
lessons.try: Mark solstices and equinoxes on an orbit diagram.

learn: When it is summer in Arizona, it is winter in Australia.
The hemispheres have opposite seasons.
The equator has little seasonal change.
check: When Arizona has summer, Australia has...
lessons.try: Compare seasons in two cities.

learn: Earth is actually closest to the sun in January.
So distance cannot cause seasons.
Tilt is the cause.
check: Earth is closest to the sun in...
The real cause of seasons is...
lessons.try: Debate and correct the distance myth.

learn: The moon reflects sunlight; half is always lit.
We see different amounts of the lit half as it orbits.
Earth's shadow does NOT cause phases.
check: Phases are caused by our ___ view of the lit half.
lessons.try: Model phases with a ball on a stick around a lamp.

learn: New, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full.
Then waning gibbous, third quarter, waning crescent.
A cycle takes about 29.5 days.
lessons.try: Order phase cards.

learn: The moon rotates once per orbit.
So the same side always faces Earth.
The far side was first photographed in 1959.
check: The far side was first photographed in...
lessons.try: Walk around a chair always facing it.

learn: The moon passes between the sun and Earth.
The moon's shadow falls on Earth.
Never look at the sun without eclipse glasses.
check: In a solar eclipse, the ___ is in the middle.
A solar eclipse happens at ___ moon.
lessons.try: Model a solar eclipse.

learn: Earth passes between the sun and moon.
Earth's shadow falls on the moon.
The moon can turn red ("blood moon").
check: In a lunar eclipse, ___ is in the middle.
A lunar eclipse happens at ___ moon.
lessons.try: Model a lunar eclipse.

learn: The moon's gravity pulls oceans into bulges.
Most coasts get two high and two low tides a day.
Spring tides (biggest) happen at new and full moons.
check: Tides are caused mainly by the...
Most coasts get ___ high tides a day.
lessons.try: Graph tide data for a coastal town.

learn: Tilt causes seasons.
Viewing angle causes phases.
Alignment causes eclipses; gravity causes tides.
check: Solar eclipse: moon between sun and...
Tides are mainly from the moon's...
lessons.try: Earth-moon-sun model show.

learn: A star is a huge ball of hot gas that makes its own light and heat.
Stars differ in size, colour and brightness. Blue stars are hottest; red stars are coolest.
The Sun is a medium-sized yellow star.
lessons.try: Look at a star chart and find a red star and a blue star.

learn: Stars form in clouds of gas and dust called nebulae.
Medium stars like the Sun swell into red giants and end as white dwarfs.
Very massive stars can end in a supernova explosion, leaving a neutron star or black hole.
check: Very massive stars can end in a...
lessons.try: Draw a flowchart of a star's life cycle.

learn: A galaxy is a huge system of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.
Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is a spiral galaxy with hundreds of billions of stars.
Distances between stars are measured in light-years: the distance light travels in one year.
check: The Milky Way is a ___ galaxy.
lessons.try: On a dark night, look for the band of the Milky Way.

learn: Stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores.
Fusion releases enormous energy.
The sun fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen each second.
lessons.try: Diagram fusion in a star's core.

learn: Blue stars are hottest; red stars are coolest.
The sun is a yellow star.
Colour reveals surface temperature.
lessons.try: Sort star cards by temperature.

learn: Apparent brightness is how bright it looks from Earth.
Absolute brightness is how bright it really is.
A close dim star can look brighter than a far bright one.
check: How bright a star looks from Earth is...
A close dim star can look ___ than a far bright one.
Absolute brightness is how bright it...
lessons.try: Compare torches at different distances.

learn: Plots stars by temperature and brightness.
Most stars, including the sun, lie on the main sequence.
Giants are bright and cool; white dwarfs are dim and hot.
check: The sun is on the main...
lessons.try: Plot ten stars on an H-R diagram.

lessons.t: Life Cycle of a Sun-Like Star
learn: Nebula → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf.
The sun will become a red giant in about 5 billion years.
It will not explode as a supernova.
check: The sun will become a red giant in about...
The sun will end as a...
lessons.try: Draw the sun's life cycle.

learn: Massive stars become red supergiants.
They explode as supernovas.
Leftovers: neutron stars or black holes.
lessons.try: Compare life cycles of small and massive stars.

lessons.t: We Are Made of Star Stuff
learn: Heavy elements like iron and carbon formed in stars.
Supernovas scattered them into space.
They became planets and living things.
check: The iron in your blood came from...
lessons.try: Trace an iron atom from a star to your blood.

learn: Constellations are patterns as seen from Earth.
Their stars may be very far apart.
Star maps change with season and latitude.
check: Stars in a constellation may be...
lessons.try: Use a star wheel to find three constellations.

learn: Our galaxy is a barred spiral with 100–400 billion stars.
The sun sits in a spiral arm.
The centre holds a supermassive black hole.
check: The Milky Way is a ___ galaxy.
The sun is in a spiral...
lessons.try: Draw the Milky Way and mark our position.

learn: Spiral, elliptical and irregular.
Andromeda is our nearest large spiral neighbour.
Galaxies contain billions of stars.
check: A galaxy with no clear shape is...
lessons.try: Sort galaxy photos by type.

learn: Edwin Hubble found galaxies moving away from us (1929).
Farther galaxies move faster.
The universe began expanding about 13.8 billion years ago.
check: The universe is about ___ years old.
lessons.try: Model expansion with dots on a balloon.

learn: Fusion powers stars.
Star life cycles depend on mass.
Galaxies and expansion.
lessons.try: Cosmic scale timeline.

units.t: Minerals, Rocks and the Rock Cycle

learn: A mineral is a naturally formed, non-living solid with a crystal structure.
Geologists identify minerals by colour, streak, lustre, hardness and cleavage.
The Mohs scale rates hardness from 1 (talc) to 10 (diamond).
check: The softest mineral on the Mohs scale is...
The colour of a mineral's powder is its...
lessons.try: Test which of your rock samples can be scratched by a fingernail or a coin.

learn: Igneous rock forms when melted rock (magma or lava) cools and hardens: granite, basalt.
Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sediment are pressed and cemented: sandstone, limestone.
Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change existing rock: marble, slate.
lessons.try: Sort a rock collection into the three kinds.

learn: The rock cycle shows how rocks change from one kind to another over long periods.
Weathering, erosion, melting, cooling, heat and pressure drive the cycle.
Any type of rock can become any other type.
lessons.try: Draw the rock cycle with arrows labelled by process.

learn: A mineral is naturally formed, inorganic, solid, with a definite chemical make-up and crystal structure.
Quartz, halite (salt) and feldspar are minerals.
Coal and pearls are not minerals.
lessons.try: Check five materials against the definition.

learn: Tests: colour, streak, lustre, hardness, cleavage, fracture.
Streak is the colour of the powder.
Colour alone can be misleading.
check: Streak is the colour of the...
lessons.try: Test five mineral samples.

learn: 1 talc to 10 diamond.
A fingernail is about 2.5; a steel nail about 5.5.
Harder scratches softer.
lessons.try: Rank minerals by scratch test.

learn: Atoms arrange in repeating patterns.
Halite forms cubes; quartz forms six-sided columns.
Slow cooling makes bigger crystals.
lessons.try: Grow salt and sugar crystals.

learn: Formed from cooled magma or lava.
Intrusive (inside Earth, coarse grains): granite.
Extrusive (on surface, fine grains): basalt, obsidian.
lessons.try: Compare granite and obsidian.

learn: Formed when sediments are deposited, compacted and cemented.
Sandstone, shale, limestone.
Often contain fossils and layers.
lessons.try: Make a sedimentary "rock" in a cup.

learn: Heat and pressure change existing rocks.
Limestone → marble; shale → slate; granite → gneiss.
They don't melt.
check: Metamorphic rocks form by heat and...
lessons.try: Match parent rocks to metamorphic rocks.

learn: Any rock can become any other type.
Weathering, melting, heat and pressure drive changes.
The cycle takes millions of years.
lessons.try: Draw a rock cycle with arrows labelled.

learn: The Grand Canyon shows sedimentary layers over a billion years.
San Francisco Peaks are volcanic.
Petrified Forest has fossil logs turned to quartz.
check: The Grand Canyon walls are mostly ___ rock.
lessons.try: Map Arizona's famous rocks.

learn: Copper (big in Arizona), iron, aluminium.
Minerals in phones, buildings and food (salt).
Mining has costs and benefits.
check: Arizona is a big producer of...
lessons.try: List minerals in a smartphone.

learn: Soil forms from weathered rock and decayed organisms.
Layers: topsoil, subsoil, bedrock.
It can take hundreds of years for an inch.
check: Soil forms from weathered rock and...
lessons.try: Examine a soil profile.

learn: Mineral properties and tests.
Three rock types and the cycle.
Rocks in Arizona and in daily life.
lessons.try: Rock identification lab.

learn: Earth has a crust, mantle, outer core and inner core.
The crust and upper mantle are broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates.
Plates move a few centimetres a year, slowly floating on the hot mantle below.
check: The thin outer layer of Earth is the...
The centre of Earth is the...
lessons.try: Label a diagram of Earth's layers.

learn: At divergent boundaries plates move apart, forming ridges and rift valleys.
At convergent boundaries plates push together, forming mountains or trenches.
At transform boundaries plates slide past each other, like the San Andreas Fault.
check: Plates moving apart is a ___ boundary.
The Himalayas formed at a ___ boundary.
The San Andreas Fault is a ___ boundary.
lessons.try: Use two pieces of foam to model each boundary type.

learn: Earthquakes happen when rocks along a fault suddenly slip, sending out seismic waves.
Volcanoes form where magma reaches the surface, often at plate boundaries or hot spots like Hawaii.
Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur around the Pacific "Ring of Fire".
check: The area around the Pacific with many quakes is the...
lessons.try: Mark recent earthquakes on a world map and look for patterns.

learn: Alfred Wegener (1912) proposed continents once formed one supercontinent, Pangaea.
Evidence: matching coastlines, fossils and rocks across oceans.
He couldn't explain how they moved.
lessons.try: Fit continent cut-outs into Pangaea.

learn: In the 1960s, scientists mapped mid-ocean ridges.
New crust forms at ridges and spreads outwards.
Magnetic stripes record Earth's field flips.
lessons.try: Model sea-floor spreading with paper strips.

learn: Hot mantle rock rises slowly; cooler rock sinks.
These convection currents help move plates.
Like a pot of thick soup.
lessons.try: Watch convection with food colouring in warm water.

learn: Plates move apart.
Mid-ocean ridges and rift valleys form.
Iceland sits on one.
lessons.try: Find divergent boundaries on a map.

learn: Plates collide.
Ocean under continent: trenches and volcanoes (the Andes).
Continent with continent: mountains (the Himalayas).
check: The Himalayas formed from two ___ plates colliding.
lessons.try: Model collisions with sponges.

learn: Plates slide past each other.
The San Andreas Fault in California.
Causes many earthquakes.
check: A famous transform fault is the...
lessons.try: Slide two blocks with rough edges.

learn: Stress builds along faults until rock snaps.
The focus is underground; the epicentre is on the surface above.
Energy travels as seismic waves.
check: The point on the surface above the focus is the...
lessons.try: Model stress with a bending ruler.

learn: Seismographs record shaking.
Magnitude scales: each whole number is about 32 times more energy.
Three stations locate the epicentre.
check: To locate an epicentre you need ___ stations.
lessons.try: Locate an epicentre by triangulation.

learn: Magma rises through cracks.
Volcanoes form at boundaries and hot spots.
Hawaii formed over a hot spot.
lessons.try: Map volcanoes and plate boundaries together.

learn: Shield (gentle, runny lava): Mauna Loa.
Composite (explosive, layered): Mount St. Helens.
Cinder cone (small, steep): Sunset Crater in Arizona.
check: Sunset Crater in Arizona is a...
Mount St. Helens is a ___ volcano.
lessons.try: Build models of the three types.

learn: A belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific.
Caused by subduction zones.
Japan, Chile and Alaska lie on it.
check: The Ring of Fire circles the ___ Ocean.
A country on the Ring of Fire:
lessons.try: Trace the Ring of Fire on a map.

learn: Drift, spreading, convection.
Three boundary types.
Earthquakes and volcanoes.
lessons.try: Plate boundary card match.

learn: Weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces.
Mechanical weathering breaks rock physically: ice wedging, roots and rubbing.
Chemical weathering changes what rock is made of, as when acidic rain dissolves limestone.
check: Ice in cracks widening rock is...
lessons.try: Find examples of weathering on buildings, pavements or gravestones.

learn: Erosion moves weathered material by water, wind, ice and gravity.
Deposition drops material in a new place, building deltas, beaches and sand dunes.
Rivers carved the Grand Canyon over millions of years.
check: Erosion is the ___ of weathered material.
The Grand Canyon was carved mainly by...
lessons.try: Build a sand slope and pour water to watch erosion.

learn: Fossils are preserved remains or traces of ancient living things, usually found in sedimentary rock.
The law of superposition says lower rock layers are usually older than layers above.
Fossils and layers help scientists build Earth's history, which is about 4.6 billion years old.
lessons.try: Make a layered model with different colours of clay and "fossils".

learn: Mechanical weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing what it is made of.
Frost wedging: water freezes in cracks, expands by about 9% and splits rock.
Roots, abrasion by sand and temperature changes also break rock.
check: Water expands about ___ when it freezes.
lessons.try: Freeze a water-filled clay ball and observe cracks.

learn: Chemical weathering changes the minerals in rock.
Acid rain dissolves limestone; oxygen rusts iron-rich rock.
Caves form when water dissolves limestone.
lessons.try: Drop vinegar on chalk and limestone.

learn: Climate, rock type and surface area affect speed.
Warm, wet climates weather rock fastest.
Many small pieces weather faster than one big block.
check: Granite weathers ___ than limestone in acid.
lessons.try: Compare sugar cubes and loose sugar dissolving.

learn: Rivers carry sediment and carve valleys.
Faster water carries bigger pieces.
The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon.
check: The Grand Canyon was carved by the ___ River.
lessons.try: Use a stream table to model erosion.

learn: Wind moves sand and dust.
It forms dunes and sculpts arches and hoodoos.
Dust storms (haboobs) sweep Arizona.
check: Wind erosion is strongest where there are few...
lessons.try: Blow sand across a tray and watch dunes form.

learn: Glaciers scrape and carry rock.
They carve U-shaped valleys.
They leave piles called moraines.
lessons.try: Drag an ice cube with gravel over clay.

learn: Landslides, mudflows and rockfalls move material downhill.
Heavy rain and steep slopes increase risk.
Plant roots help hold soil.
lessons.try: Model a landslide with wet and dry sand.

learn: When water or wind slows, it drops sediment.
Deltas, sandbars and dunes are deposits.
Larger pieces drop first.
lessons.try: Watch sediment settle in a jar.

learn: Fossils are remains or traces of ancient life.
Most form in sedimentary rock.
Types: mould, cast, petrified, trace, amber.
check: Most fossils are found in ___ rock.
lessons.try: Make a mould and cast fossil with clay and plaster.

learn: In undisturbed layers, the oldest is at the bottom.
Younger layers are on top.
Used for relative dating.
check: The oldest layer is usually at the...
lessons.try: Order layers in a diagram.

learn: Index fossils lived for short times over wide areas.
They help match layers across places.
Radioactive dating gives ages in years.
lessons.try: Match rock layers using index fossils.

learn: Earth is about 4.6 billion years old.
Eras: Precambrian, Paleozoic, Mesozoic (dinosaurs), Cenozoic (mammals).
Humans appeared very recently.
lessons.try: Make a toilet-paper timeline of Earth's history.

units.t: The Water Cycle and Earth’s Water

learn: The Sun's energy drives the water cycle.
Water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation, and collects as runoff and groundwater.
Plants also release water vapour through transpiration.
lessons.try: Make a mini water cycle in a sealed bag taped to a sunny window.

learn: About 97% of Earth's water is salty ocean water.
Most fresh water is frozen in glaciers and ice caps; only a small part is easy to use.
Groundwater fills spaces in rock underground in layers called aquifers.
lessons.try: Use 100 cups of water to model how much is fresh and usable.

learn: Ocean currents move huge amounts of water around the world.
Surface currents are driven by wind; deep currents by differences in temperature and saltiness.
Currents carry heat and affect climate, like the Gulf Stream warming western Europe.
check: Surface currents are driven mostly by...
lessons.try: Trace the Gulf Stream on a world map.

learn: The sun's energy evaporates water; gravity pulls it back down.
Each year about 500,000 km³ of water evaporates.
The cycle has no start or end.
lessons.try: Draw the water cycle with energy arrows.

learn: Plants release water vapour through leaves.
A large oak can transpire about 150,000 litres a year.
Transpiration and evaporation together are evapotranspiration.
lessons.try: Bag a leafy branch and collect water.

learn: Air cools until it can't hold its vapour: the dew point.
Vapour condenses on dust to form cloud droplets.
Dew forms on cool grass at night.
check: The temperature where condensation starts is the...
lessons.try: Find the dew point with a can of ice water.

learn: Cumulus: puffy. Stratus: flat sheets. Cirrus: wispy and high.
Cumulonimbus are storm clouds.
Clouds help forecast weather.
lessons.try: Keep a cloud journal for a week.

learn: Water soaks into soil (infiltration).
It fills spaces in rock: the saturated zone.
The top of this zone is the water table.
check: The top of the saturated zone is the...
lessons.try: Test how fast water soaks into sand, clay and gravel.

learn: Aquifers are rock layers that hold and transmit water.
Wells tap aquifers.
Pumping faster than refilling lowers the water table.
lessons.try: Model overpumping with a cup aquifer.

learn: A watershed drains to one outlet.
Divides separate watersheds.
The Continental Divide splits North America's flow.
check: The ___ Divide splits North America's flow.
lessons.try: Trace your local watershed.

learn: Sources: Colorado River, Salt and Verde Rivers, groundwater.
The Central Arizona Project canal carries Colorado water to Phoenix and Tucson.
Drought makes conservation vital.
check: The CAP canal carries water from the ___ River.
lessons.try: Map where your tap water comes from.

learn: Ocean water averages about 3.5% salt.
Salt comes from weathered rocks carried by rivers.
Evaporation makes water saltier.
check: An egg floats better in ___ water.
lessons.try: Compare floating an egg in fresh and salt water.

learn: Surface layer is warm and mixed by wind.
The thermocline is where temperature drops fast.
The deep zone is cold and dark.
lessons.try: Graph temperature versus depth.

learn: Surface currents are driven by wind.
Deep currents are driven by density (cold, salty water sinks).
The Gulf Stream warms western Europe.
lessons.try: Model density currents with coloured salt water.

learn: Sun and gravity drive the cycle.
Groundwater, rivers, oceans.
Arizona's water and conservation.
check: The water table is the top of the ___ zone.
lessons.try: Water journey role-play.

learn: The atmosphere is a layer of gases around Earth, mostly nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%).
Weather happens in the lowest layer, the troposphere.
The ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs harmful ultraviolet light.
lessons.try: Draw the layers of the atmosphere.

learn: Air masses are large bodies of air with similar temperature and humidity.
A front is the boundary where two air masses meet.
Cold fronts often bring quick storms; warm fronts bring steady rain.
check: The boundary between air masses is a...
lessons.try: Read a weather map and find a cold front and a warm front.

learn: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a place and time.
Climate is the average weather pattern over many years.
Latitude, altitude, oceans and mountains all affect climate.
check: Places near the equator are usually...
lessons.try: Compare the climate of your town with a town near the equator.

learn: Troposphere (weather), stratosphere (ozone layer), mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere.
Air thins with height.
The ozone layer absorbs harmful UV.
check: The ozone layer is in the...
lessons.try: Build a layered atmosphere poster.

learn: Air has weight and presses on everything.
Barometers measure pressure.
Falling pressure often means storms.
check: Air pressure is measured with a...
lessons.try: Make a jar barometer.

learn: The equator gets more direct sunlight than the poles.
Land heats and cools faster than water.
Uneven heating creates wind.
lessons.try: Heat sand and water under a lamp and compare.

learn: Wind blows from high to low pressure.
Sea breezes blow onshore by day; land breezes offshore at night.
Anemometers measure wind speed.
check: Wind blows from ___ to low pressure.
A daytime breeze from the sea is a ___ breeze.
Wind speed is measured with an...
lessons.try: Build an anemometer.

lessons.t: Global Winds and the Coriolis Effect
learn: Earth's spin curves winds (Coriolis effect).
Trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies.
Westerlies move U.S. weather west to east.
check: Earth's spin curves winds through the ___ effect.
lessons.try: Draw global wind belts.

learn: Humidity is water vapour in air.
Relative humidity compares it to the most air can hold.
Arizona's air is often very dry.
lessons.try: Make a hair hygrometer.

learn: Large bodies of air with similar temperature and humidity.
Maritime (wet) or continental (dry); tropical (warm) or polar (cold).
They bring weather where they move.
check: A wet air mass forms over...
lessons.try: Label air masses on a U.S. map.

learn: Fronts are boundaries between air masses.
Cold fronts bring quick storms; warm fronts bring steady rain.
Map symbols: blue triangles (cold), red half-circles (warm).
check: A front is a boundary between...
lessons.try: Read fronts on a weather map.

learn: Thunderstorms, tornadoes, hurricanes.
Lightning heats air to about 30,000 °C, causing thunder.
Arizona's monsoon brings storms and flash floods.
lessons.try: Make a severe weather safety guide.
